# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting close to red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may freeze out entirely. On the exoplanet WASP-96b... wait, let me reconsider—WASP-96b is not tidally locked in the classic sense.

Better examples include the exoplanet LHS 3844b, where models suggest the dayside reaches 800°C while the nightside remains airless and frozen. Even more relevant are potentially habitable "eyeball Earths"—worlds where the substellar point hosts a permanent ocean beneath a thick atmosphere, surrounded by rings of ice on the nightward side.

Atmospheric and oceanic heat transport becomes the critical factor determining whether such planets remain habitable. A dense atmosphere can redistribute heat effectively, moderating both hemispheres.
